Tasks to be Carried Out This Week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material Monday App Modernization & Serverless Backend: - Architecting serverless backends with Lambda, S3, DynamoDB (000078). - Secure identity management and authentication with Amazon Cognito (000081). - Automated serverless packaging with AWS SAM (000080). 09/28/2026 09/28/2026 Cloud Journey - Modernize Tuesday Enterprise Container Services & Managed Kubernetes: - Microservices containerization via Amazon ECS Fargate (000067). - Managed Kubernetes clusters with Amazon EKS (000126). - Hybrid cloud operations via Red Hat OpenShift on AWS - ROSA (000071). 09/29/2026 09/29/2026 Cloud Journey - Containers Wednesday Data Analytics & Modern Cloud Data Lakes: - Establishing cloud data lake architectures with Data Lake Fundamentals (000035). - Serverless interactive querying using Amazon Athena (000106). - Business intelligence dashboards via Amazon QuickSight (000073). 09/30/2026 09/30/2026 Cloud Journey - Data Thursday Hands-On Amazon RDS Deployment (Primary Focus): - Provisioning a multi-AZ VPC segregating Public Web and Private Database subnets. - Implementing chained Security Group rules authorizing MySQL port 3306. - Deploying Amazon RDS MySQL Multi-AZ instances and validating EC2 client connectivity. - Executing manual snapshots and practicing disaster recovery restoration drills. 10/01/2026 10/01/2026 Amazon RDS Workshop (000005) Friday Week 3 Review, Worklog Completion & Proposal Submission: - Knowledge Review: Consolidate serverless patterns, container ecosystems, analytics, and RDS Multi-AZ. - Worklog Completion: Finalize comprehensive documentation for lab 1.3.1 and synthesize Week 3 logs. - Project Work: Perform final review and officially submit the formal Capstone Project Proposal. 10/02/2026 10/02/2026 The First Cloud Journey Daily In-Depth Learning Outcomes & Key Takeaways: 📌 Monday (09/28/2026) - Application Modernization & Serverless Backend What did we learn today? Three-Tier Serverless Web Architecture: Mastered decoupled serverless patterns: Client-side single-page applications hosted on Amazon S3 ➔ Business logic execution via Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda ➔ Persistent low-latency data storage on Amazon DynamoDB. Identity Lifecycle Governance with Amazon Cognito: Configured Cognito User Pools: Managed user registration, login authentication, email OTP verification, password resets, and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA). Configured Cognito Identity Pools: Enabled federated identity mapping, vending short-lived temporary AWS STS credentials granting authenticated end-users direct access to scoped AWS resources (such as uploading user profile photos to dedicated S3 user prefixes). Infrastructure as Code via AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model): Authored concise declarative template.yaml manifests defining Lambda handlers, DynamoDB tables, and API routes, automating compilation and deployment via sam build and sam deploy. Figure 1.3.1: Serverless event-driven architecture orchestrating AWS Lambda and downstream managed services.
Figure 1.3.2: Centralized user authentication and granular authorization model via Amazon Cognito and IAM Roles.
Encountered Challenges & Solutions: API Gateway Token Validation Rejections: Client requests passing Cognito JWT tokens received HTTP 401 Unauthorized. Root cause: The HTTP Authorization request header omitted the mandatory Bearer prefix. Solution: Standardized the client request interceptor to transmit headers strictly formatted as Bearer <id_token>. 📌 Tuesday (09/29/2026) - Enterprise Container Services & Kubernetes What did we learn today? Microservices Decomposition with Amazon ECS Fargate: Explored decomposing legacy monolithic architectures into decoupled service tasks (Authentication, Product Catalog, Order Processing), containerizing workloads with Docker, and running on serverless AWS Fargate infrastructure with independent scaling policies. Managed Kubernetes on Amazon EKS: Evaluated industrial Kubernetes primitives: Pods, Services, Deployments, ReplicaSets, and Ingress controllers. Analyzed how EKS manages a highly available multi-AZ control plane, ensuring open-standard container workload portability without proprietary vendor lock-in. Enterprise Hybrid Platforms with ROSA: Evaluated Red Hat OpenShift on AWS (ROSA), delivering a unified, managed OpenShift experience that bridges on-premises enterprise data centers with public cloud infrastructure. Figure 1.3.3: Multi-tier microservices container architecture operating on Amazon ECS backed by AWS Fargate.
Encountered Challenges & Solutions: Container Orchestration Platform Selection: Evaluated decision criteria between ECS and EKS. Takeaway: Adopt Amazon ECS Fargate when teams prioritize operational simplicity, tight AWS service integration, and lower administrative overhead; Adopt Amazon EKS when organizations maintain existing Kubernetes operational expertise, require complex Helm ecosystem tooling, or mandate multi-cloud deployment parity. 📌 Wednesday (09/30/2026) - Cloud Data Lakes & Business Intelligence What did we learn today? Modern Data Lake Architectural Principles: Analyzed the benefits of breaking data silos by consolidating structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data into an immutable Amazon S3 lake, decoupling storage capacity from analytical compute engines. Automated Data Cataloging with AWS Glue: Configured Glue Crawlers to scan S3 raw log directories, automatically inferring record schemas and registering partition metadata within the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Distributed SQL Queries & Visual Analytics: Executed serverless ANSI SQL queries against raw datasets via Amazon Athena without managing relational database servers, piping query results directly into Amazon QuickSight to render interactive operational charts. Figure 1.3.4: End-to-end data lake pipeline from ingestion and S3 storage to Glue cataloging and QuickSight visualization.
Encountered Challenges & Solutions: Escalating Query Costs on Raw CSV Datasets: Running repeated SELECT queries across multi-gigabyte uncompressed CSV files resulted in full-table scans. Solution: Applied the best practice of transforming data into columnar Apache Parquet format with Snappy compression and chronological partitioning, reducing scanned data volumes by over 90%. 📌 Thursday (10/01/2026) - Hands-On Amazon RDS Deployment The Deploying Relational Databases with Amazon RDS lab was executed on Thursday (01/10/2026) as part of Week 3. This page provides comprehensive technical documentation for designing a highly available, multi-Availability Zone (Multi-AZ) two-tier network architecture, configuring chained security group firewalls, provisioning an Amazon RDS MySQL instance, connecting an Amazon EC2 Web Server, and executing data protection workflows via Manual DB Snapshots and Point-in-Time Restore. 🔗 Lab Reference Source: Get Started with Amazon RDS Workshop
🎯 Lab Objectives: Master the architecture, high availability mechanisms, and operational best practices of Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service). Design and implement an isolated Two-Tier Architecture: placing the Web Server tier in a Public Subnet and the Database tier in isolated Private Subnets to enforce defense-in-depth security principles. Create a DB Subnet Group spanning across at least two distinct Availability Zones (us-east-1a and us-east-1b) to satisfy Multi-AZ high-availability requirements. Configure granular network isolation via Security Groups: restricting the MySQL inbound port TCP 3306 exclusively to traffic originating from the Web Server’s Security Group (ec2-sg), prohibiting direct ingress from the public Internet. Provision an Amazon RDS database utilizing the MySQL Community Edition engine, configured on the db.m5.large instance class with automated synchronous Multi-AZ Deployment enabled. Deploy an Amazon EC2 web workstation (Amazon Linux 2023), install Apache HTTP Server and the PHP runtime, configure connection strings to the private RDS Endpoint, and validate end-to-end CRUD operations. Execute database snapshot protection through Manual DB Snapshots, analyze automated daily backup windows, and understand disaster recovery workflows (Point-in-Time Recovery - PITR). 📊 Provisioned Resource Specifications: Parameter / Resource Actual Value Technical Significance & Role Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) rds-vpc (vpc-0d0b88a31c814b1df) Isolated virtual network environment with CIDR block 10.0.0.0/16 Public Subnet rds-subnet-public1-us-east-1a Public-facing subnet associated with an Internet Gateway, auto-assigns Public IPs Private Subnet 1 rds-subnet-private1-us-east-1a Isolated private subnet in us-east-1a hosting the Primary DB instance Private Subnet 2 rds-subnet-private2-us-east-1b Isolated private subnet in us-east-1b hosting the Standby DB replica DB Subnet Group rds-subnet-group Multi-AZ subnet collection designated for RDS database failover Web Security Group ec2-sg (sg-0cec4d0fbfc6d4c41) Inbound: Port 80 (HTTP from 0.0.0.0/0) & Port 22 (SSH from My IP) RDS Security Group rds-sg (sg-0331b33d6bf62d714) Inbound: Port 3306 (MySQL) restricted strictly to ec2-sg RDS Instance Identifier db-instance MySQL Community 8.0, Instance Class: db.m5.large (2 vCPUs, 8 GiB RAM) Deployment Mode Multi-AZ Deployment Synchronous secondary replica in another AZ for automatic seamless failover Database Name fcaj Initial database created upon deployment Master Username admin Root administrative credential for database management RDS Endpoint db-instance.cgnkaue6ib4x.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com Private canonical DNS endpoint resolving to port 3306 Web Server Instance web-server t2.micro, Amazon Linux 2023, Apache httpd & PHP 🏛️ Architecture Overview: The deployment adheres strictly to the AWS Well-Architected Framework:
📋 Detailed Step-by-Step Implementation Guide: 🔹 Module 1: Architecture Design & Network Infrastructure Preparation Step 1: Provision the Multi-AZ VPC (rds-vpc) Action: Sign in to the AWS Management Console ➔ Navigate to VPC ➔ Click Create VPC. Configuration: Select VPC and more for automated network topology creation. Name tag: rds-vpc IPv4 CIDR block: 10.0.0.0/16 Number of Availability Zones (AZs): 2 (us-east-1a and us-east-1b) Number of public subnets: 2 Number of private subnets: 2 NAT gateways: None (to eliminate unnecessary operational cost during lab testing) VPC Endpoints: None Action: Click Create VPC and verify completion across all network routing components. Step 2: Enable Public IPv4 Addressing for the Public Subnet Action: Go to Subnets ➔ Select rds-subnet-public1-us-east-1a ➔ Select Actions ➔ Edit subnet settings. Configuration: Check Enable auto-assign public IPv4 address ➔ Click Save. Objective: Ensures any web tier EC2 instances launched in this subnet automatically receive routable public IP addresses for incoming user traffic. 🔹 Module 2: Configuring Security Group Firewalls & DB Subnet Group Step 3: Configure Web Server Security Group (ec2-sg) Action: Navigate to Security Groups ➔ Click Create security group. Settings: Security group name: ec2-sg VPC: Select rds-vpc Inbound rules: Rule 1: Type HTTP, Port 80, Source 0.0.0.0/0 (allows general public access). Rule 2: Type SSH, Port 22, Source My IP (secures administrative shell access). Step 4: Configure Database Security Group (rds-sg) Action: Click Create security group again. Settings: Security group name: rds-sg VPC: Select rds-vpc Inbound rules: Type MySQL/Aurora, Port 3306, Source select Custom ➔ Enter the Security Group ID of ec2-sg (sg-0cec4d0fbfc6d4c41). Security Significance: Known as Chained Security Groups, this pattern ensures that no unauthorized machine from the Internet or within the VPC can connect to port 3306 unless it explicitly carries the ec2-sg tag. Step 5: Create DB Subnet Group Action: Open the Amazon RDS console ➔ Click Subnet groups ➔ Click Create DB subnet group. Settings: Name: rds-subnet-group Description: Subnet group for RDS MySQL Multi-AZ VPC: Select rds-vpc Availability Zones: Select both us-east-1a and us-east-1b. Subnets: Select the two Private Subnets associated with the selected AZs (10.0.128.0/20 and 10.0.144.0/20). Action: Click Create. 🔹 Module 3: Provisioning & Configuring Amazon RDS MySQL Multi-AZ Step 6: Launch the Amazon RDS Instance Action: In the Amazon RDS console, click Databases ➔ Click Create database. Detailed Configuration Parameters: Database creation method: Standard create Engine options: MySQL (Community Edition 8.0) Templates: Production (enables the Multi-AZ configuration) Deployment options: Multi-AZ DB instance (Creates primary instance and synchronous standby replica) DB instance identifier: db-instance Master username: admin Master password: Set strong credentials DB instance class: Standard classes db.m5.large (2 vCPUs, 8 GiB RAM) Storage: General Purpose SSD (gp2/gp3), Allocated storage 20 GiB Virtual Private Cloud (VPC): rds-vpc DB subnet group: rds-subnet-group Public access: No (Enforces private internal network isolation) VPC security group: Choose rds-sg (remove the default group) Initial database name: fcaj Action: Click Create database and allow 10 to 15 minutes for complete automated provisioning. Step 7: Inspect Operational Logs, Events, and Automated Maintenance Observations: In the Connectivity & security tab, record the canonical Endpoint and Port 3306. In the Logs & events tab, inspect provisioning audit trails, initial automated snapshots, and synchronous replica creation logs. In the Maintenance & backups tab, verify that automated backups are enabled with a 7-day retention period and examine the scheduled maintenance window. 🔹 Module 4: Deploying Web Server (EC2) & Establishing Database Connectivity Step 8: Launch the EC2 Web Instance Action: Navigate to EC2 ➔ Click Launch instances. Parameters: Name: web-server AMI: Amazon Linux 2023 AMI Instance type: t2.micro Network settings: VPC rds-vpc, Subnet rds-subnet-public1-us-east-1a, Auto-assign Public IP: Enable, Security group: ec2-sg. Step 9: Install the Web Stack and Test Database Connectivity Action: Establish SSH connection into the EC2 instance via terminal: # Update software packages sudo dnf update -y # Install Apache HTTP Server, MariaDB client, and PHP MySQL extensions sudo dnf install -y httpd php php-mysqli php-pdo mariadb105 # Start and enable the Apache service sudo systemctl start httpd sudo systemctl enable httpd Verify network line of sight from EC2 to RDS: # Test TCP handshake on port 3306 nc -zv db-instance.cgnkaue6ib4x.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com 3306 Deploy PHP database verification script (/var/www/html/dbtest.php): <?php $servername = "db-instance.cgnkaue6ib4x.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com"; $username = "admin"; $password = "YourMasterPassword123"; $dbname = "fcaj"; // Create connection $conn = new mysqli($servername, $username, $password, $dbname); // Check connection if ($conn->connect_error) { die("Database connection failed: " . $conn->connect_error); } echo "<h1>Amazon RDS Database Connection Successful!</h1>"; echo "<p>Connected securely to database: <strong>" . $dbname . "</strong> via internal endpoint.</p>"; $conn->close(); ?> Validation: Open a web browser and navigate to: http://<EC2-Public-IP>/dbtest.php. The success banner validates flawless end-to-end multi-tier connectivity. 🔹 Module 5: Operational Resilience & Data Protection (Snapshot Backup & Restore) Step 10: Create a Manual DB Snapshot Action: In the Amazon RDS console ➔ Select db-instance ➔ Click Actions ➔ Take snapshot. Parameters: Snapshot name: rds-manual-snapshot-fcaj Action: Click Take snapshot. Architectural Purpose: Manual snapshots are stored durably in internal Amazon S3 storage across multiple AZs and persist until explicitly deleted by administrators, even if the source DB instance is terminated. Step 11: Database Recovery Workflow (Restore from Snapshot) Standard AWS Recovery Lifecycle: To initiate a restore, select the snapshot rds-manual-snapshot-fcaj ➔ Click Actions ➔ Restore snapshot. AWS creates a brand-new DB Instance with a distinct DNS endpoint, ensuring the production database is not accidentally overwritten. Once data integrity verification is completed, web tier connection strings are updated to point to the new endpoint to complete the disaster recovery cutover. 💡 Troubleshooting & Real-World Lessons: 1. Connection Timed Out Between Web Server and RDS Root Cause: Inbound security group rules on rds-sg did not permit port 3306 from the ec2-sg security group ID, or the RDS instance was placed in subnets lacking local route connectivity to the public subnet. Troubleshooting: Use nc -zv <RDS-Endpoint> 3306 directly from the EC2 shell to confirm Transport Layer connectivity before inspecting application application code. 2. Subnet Group Availability Zone Constraint Error Root Cause: When configuring Multi-AZ deployment, Amazon RDS enforces that the DB Subnet Group must cover at least two distinct Availability Zones. Resolution: Ensure that when creating rds-subnet-group, at least two subnets in separate AZs (e.g., us-east-1a and us-east-1b) are included. 3. High Availability Failover vs. Read Scalability Multi-AZ: Designed for High Availability (HA). The standby replica is an exact synchronous copy that does not accept read or write traffic. In a failure event, automated DNS failover redirects traffic to the standby within 60–120 seconds. Read Replicas: Designed for Read Scalability. They utilize asynchronous replication and expose individual endpoints to offload heavy analytical read traffic from the primary instance. 4. Cost Optimization & Resource Teardown Best Practice: The db.m5.large Multi-AZ configuration incurs notable hourly operational expenses. Upon finishing lab testing, create a final snapshot if data preservation is needed, and terminate the instance to prevent unnecessary charges. 📌 Summary & Skills Acquired: Through the Deploying Relational Databases with Amazon RDS lab, the intern has acquired:
End-to-end mastery in architecting secure, isolated multi-tier database topologies in the AWS Cloud. Hands-on proficiency in chained security group configurations and DB Subnet Group provisioning. Complete command over high-availability Multi-AZ failover and disaster recovery snapshot procedures. What did we learn today? Secure Two-Tier Network Architecture: Deployed VPC rds-vpc (10.0.0.0/16) spanning 4 subnets across 2 Availability Zones: 2 Public Subnets hosting EC2 Web Servers and 2 Private Subnets dedicated strictly to Amazon RDS. Ensured database instances possess zero public IP addresses and zero default internet routes, eliminating external attack vectors. Security Group Chaining: Hardened network perimeters by configuring the database security group rds-sg to authorize inbound MySQL traffic (port 3306) exclusively from the security group ID of the web server ec2-sg (sg-0cec4d0fbfc6d4c41), eliminating static IP whitelisting. High Availability with Amazon RDS Multi-AZ: Provisioned a DB Subnet Group rds-subnet-group containing private subnets across us-east-1a and us-east-1b. Launched a MySQL Community database (db.m5.large) with Multi-AZ replication. AWS maintains a primary instance while synchronously replicating storage blocks to an active standby instance in the secondary zone. In the event of an infrastructure outage, automated failover executes in under 60 seconds without client DNS reconfiguration. Disaster Recovery via Point-in-Time Recovery & Snapshots: Mastered continuous automated daily backups supporting Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) to any second within the retention window. Executed an explicit Manual Snapshot, stored durably in S3, and executed a complete restore drill to provision an independent replacement instance from the snapshot. Figure 1.3.5: Secure Two-Tier architecture separating EC2 Web Servers from private Amazon RDS database clusters.
Figure 1.3.6: Amazon RDS MySQL Multi-AZ database cluster in available status.
Encountered Challenges & Solutions: EC2 Client Connection Timeouts to Database Endpoint: Executing mysql -h <rds-endpoint> -u admin -p timed out. Root cause: The EC2 instance was assigned a default security group instead of ec2-sg, failing the security group chaining rule. Solution: Attached ec2-sg to the web instance, immediately enabling successful client database handshakes. 📌 Friday (10/02/2026) - Week 3 Review, Worklog Finalization & Proposal Submission What did we learn today? Foundational Milestone Synthesis: Completed a holistic review of the 3-week foundation: Core infrastructure (IAM, VPC, EC2, S3) ➔ Well-Architected governance (Lambda, KMS, WAF, Fargate, Savings Plans) ➔ Application modernization, containers, analytics, and relational database engineering with Amazon RDS Multi-AZ. Bilingual Worklog Consolidation: Finalized the standalone hands-on report 1.3.1. Hands-On Amazon RDS Deployment, validating 10 architectural diagrams, configuration tables, and terminal execution evidence. Official Submission of the Capstone Project Proposal: Completed final architectural verifications, risk mitigation plans, and monthly budget estimates, formally submitting the graduation Capstone Project Proposal for mentor review.

title: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL 16 Setup
content:
In this section, we deploy an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL 16.13-R2 database (exammaker-dev-pg) isolated inside 2 Private Subnets (aem-private-a and aem-private-b) of aem-demo-vpc, using the ARM64 Graviton db.t4g.micro instance class, 20 GiB gp3 storage, aws/rds encryption ($0), and 3-day automated backups.
1. Create DB Subnet Group Step 1: Create a DB Subnet Group Across 2 Availability Zones Open Aurora and RDS → select Subnet groups → Create DB subnet group. Configure the subnet group settings: Name: exammaker-dev-db-subnets Description: Private DB subnet group for AI Exam Maker (dev) VPC: aem-demo-vpc (10.20.0.0/16 — 3 Subnets, 3 Availability Zones) Availability Zones: select 2 AZs (ap-southeast-1b and ap-southeast-1c). Step 2: Attach Only the 2 Private Subnets (Isolated from Internet) Select strictly the 2 Private Subnets with no Internet Gateway route (and zero NAT Gateways, saving over $32/month):
Private Subnet 1 (aem-private-a): AZ ap-southeast-1b · CIDR 10.20.11.0/24 Private Subnet 2 (aem-private-b): AZ ap-southeast-1c · CIDR 10.20.12.0/24 Click Create to finish.
2. Select PostgreSQL 16 Engine, Single-AZ & Credentials Step 1: Choose Creation Method & Template Open Aurora and RDS → Databases → Create database. Select: Database creation method: Full configuration Engine type: PostgreSQL Templates: Dev/Test Step 2: Select Single-AZ Deployment for Cost Efficiency Under Availability and durability, select Single-AZ DB instance deployment (1 instance) (99.5% uptime, MultiAZ = false) to avoid doubling hourly compute costs during dev/demo.
Step 3: Select PostgreSQL 16 Version & Master Credentials Engine version: PostgreSQL 16.13-R2 (Disable RDS Extended Support to avoid extra extended-support fees). DB instance identifier: exammaker-dev-pg Master username: exammaker_admin Credentials management: Self managed (master password stored securely as a SecureString in SSM Parameter Store). 3. Configure db.t4g.micro, gp3 20 GiB & Private Network Step 1: Select db.t4g.micro Instance Class & gp3 Storage DB instance class: select Burstable classes (includes t classes) → db.t4g.micro (2 vCPUs, 1 GiB RAM, EBS Bandwidth up to 2,085 Mbps, Network up to 5 Gbps, ~$0.020/hour). Storage type & Capacity: General Purpose SSD (gp3), Allocated storage = 20 GiB (Baseline 3,000 IOPS, 125 MiBps). Storage autoscaling: Enabled, capped at Maximum storage threshold = 40 GiB to prevent runaway storage costs. Step 2: Configure Private Connectivity & Security Group VPC: aem-demo-vpc DB subnet group: exammaker-dev-db-subnets Public access: No (never expose the database with a Public IP). VPC security group: select aem-rds-sg (allows TCP port 5432 strictly from the backend EC2 Security Group). 4. Configure Database exammaker, Encryption & Backup Configure Initial Database, KMS Encryption & Automated Backups Expand Additional configuration and set the security and backup parameters:
Initial database name: exammaker DB parameter group: default.postgres16 (enforces encrypted connections via rds.force_ssl = 1). Encryption: Enable encryption using the AWS managed KMS key (default) aws/rds ($0). Automated Backup: Enabled Backup retention period: 3 days (stays well within the 20 GB free backup storage allocation). Backup window: 13:00 UTC (20:00 Vietnam time), Duration = 0.5 hours (30 minutes). Click Create database to launch exammaker-dev-pg.

🎯 Lab Objectives: Familiarize with the simplified management console and core capabilities of Amazon Lightsail. Provision and manage a standalone Managed Relational Database (MySQL) on Lightsail. Deploy two web applications: WordPress and Prestashop (E-Commerce) connecting to the shared database. Configure the underlying Linux/Ubuntu environment, assign Static IPs, and define firewall rules. Implement data backup procedures using Snapshots and scale up workloads by upgrading instance plans (Migration). 📊 Provisioned Resource Specifications: Resource Name / Identifier Configuration & Detailed Specs Address / Ports Notes Lightsail Database Workshop-DB-Instance MySQL 8.0, Standard Plan ($15/mo, 1GB RAM, 2 vCPUs) Port 3306, Master User: LightsailAdmin Master DB: dbWordPress WordPress Instance WordPress-1 Blueprint: WordPress (Bitnami), Linux/Ubuntu Static IP: Attached, Port 80, 443 Connected to Lightsail DB Prestashop Instance Prestashop-1 Blueprint: Prestashop, Linux/Ubuntu Static IP: Attached, Port 80, 443 E-Commerce Platform Instance Snapshot wordpress-backup-snapshot Full point-in-time snapshot before instance upgrade Size: ~20 GB, Status: Available Used for scale-up Migrated Instance WordPress-Migrated Created from Snapshot, higher hardware bundle Static IP: Re-attached Seamless service continuity 🚀 Step-by-Step Implementation & Screenshot Gallery: Step 1: Provision a Managed Relational Database (MySQL) Action / Navigation: Log into the Amazon Lightsail console ➔ Navigate to the Databases tab ➔ Click Create database. Commands Executed: # Install CloudWatch Agent package sudo yum install -y amazon-cloudwatch-agent # Start CloudWatch Agent daemon with configuration file sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl \ -a fetch-config -m ec2 -s -c file:/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 1:
If the EC2 instance lacks the CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy IAM Role, log writes in /var/log/amazon/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.log will fail with an AccessDeniedException. Always ensure IAM Role assignment prior to starting the agent service.
Step 2: Explore CloudWatch All Metrics Dashboard Action / Navigation: In the CloudWatch Console ➔ Sidebar select Metrics ➔ All metrics. Purpose: Inspect default namespaces populated automatically by AWS (e.g., AWS/EC2, AWS/EBS, AWS/ApplicationELB). Step 3: Select Per-Instance EC2 Telemetry Metrics Action / Navigation: Under All metrics, navigate to EC2 ➔ Click Per-Instance Metrics. Configuration: Locate the target Instance ID and check CPUUtilization, NetworkIn, and DiskReadBytes. Step 4: Customize Metric Visualization (Graphed Metrics) Action / Navigation: Switch to the Graphed metrics tab. Configuration: Toggle line visibility, assign unique colors, and associate series with left or right Y-axes. Step 5: Adjust Aggregation Period and Statistics Action / Navigation: Under the Statistic column, change to Average. Under Period, select 1 Minute for high-resolution sampling. Step 6: Render High-Fidelity Real-Time CPU Graph Action / Navigation: Adjust the time-window selector to 1h (last 1 hour). Observation: The plot details granular 1-minute CPU variations in real time. Step 7: Define Dynamic Search Expression Query Action / Navigation: In Graphed metrics, click Add math ➔ Search expression. Search Expression Syntax: SEARCH(' {AWS/EC2,InstanceId} MetricName="CPUUtilization" ', 'Average', 300) Purpose: Dynamically discovers and plots CPU utilization across all current and future EC2 instances without manual selection. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 7:
Search Expression syntax is sensitive to spacing and curly brace syntax {} for dimensions. Ensure metric and dimension names match exact casing (MetricName="CPUUtilization").
Step 8: Multi-Instance Telemetry Visualization via Search Expression Action / Navigation: Click Apply. Observation: The graph renders discrete lines for all active instances in the region automatically. Step 9: Audit Matched Metric Streams Action / Navigation: Expand the query results below the chart. Observation: All matching instance telemetry streams are indexed with associated Instance IDs. Step 10: Apply Mathematical Expressions to Metric Series Action / Navigation: Click Add math ➔ Start with empty expression. Formula Applied: (m1 / 100) * 100 Purpose: Normalizes data scales or computes ratios across distinct network interfaces. Step 11: Configure Dynamic Labels from Resource Properties Action / Navigation: In the Label column, enter the property interpolation variable. Expression Syntax: ${PROP('Dim.InstanceId')} - CPU Load Purpose: Replaces cryptic metric identifiers with human-readable instance IDs in the chart legend. Step 12: Validate Formatted Dashboard Graph Action / Navigation: Review the finalized graph. Observation: The legend renders dynamic contextual labels, ready to pin to an executive dashboard. Step 13: Access CloudWatch Logs Groups Console Action / Navigation: In the sidebar, select Logs ➔ Log groups. Selection: Open the /aws/ec2/system-logs log group ingested by the CloudWatch Agent. Step 14: Inspect Per-Instance Log Streams Action / Navigation: Inside /aws/ec2/system-logs, select the Log streams tab. Observation: Dedicated streams are partitioned per EC2 Instance ID. Step 15: Review Raw System Log Event Records Action / Navigation: Click a specific log stream to review raw event rows. Observation: Operating system events, boot logs, and application outputs are preserved with UTC/Local timestamps. Step 16: Launch CloudWatch Logs Insights Query Editor Action / Navigation: Sidebar select Logs ➔ Logs Insights. Configuration: In Select log group(s), choose /aws/ec2/system-logs. Step 17: Execute Query to Filter Error Messages Action / Navigation: Input the error extraction query. Query Syntax: fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /(?i)(error|exception|fail)/ | sort @timestamp desc | limit 20 Next Action: Click Run query. Step 18: Analyze Logs Insights Tabular Results Action / Navigation: Examine the tabular records returned by the query engine. Observation: Matching error events are isolated with timestamp and message payloads. Step 19: Visualize Error Occurrence Frequency Over Time Action / Navigation: Switch to the Visualization tab ➔ Select Line chart. Observation: Error volume over time displays spike frequencies clearly. Step 20: Aggregate Distribution by HTTP Status Code Action / Navigation: Execute an aggregation query across HTTP response codes. Query Syntax: stats count(*) by status_code Result: Breaks down requests into 200 (OK), 404 (Not Found), and 500 (Server Error) buckets. Step 21: Parse Custom Log Fields (Pattern Extraction) Action / Navigation: Use the parse command to extract IP, method, and URI from raw web logs. Query Syntax: parse @message "* * [*] \"* * *\" * *" as client_ip, user, timestamp, method, uri, protocol, status, bytes | display client_ip, method, uri, status Step 22: Query Top Ingress Client IP Addresses Action / Navigation: Extract and sort the highest-frequency requester IP addresses. Query Syntax: stats count(*) as request_count by client_ip | sort request_count desc | limit 10 Step 23: Save Optimized Query to Library Action / Navigation: Click Save in the top right ➔ Name the query Top-Error-Analysis. Step 24: Re-load Query from Saved Queries Pane Action / Navigation: Select the Queries tab to reload and execute previously curated queries. Step 25: Inspect Event Record Metadata and Details Action / Navigation: Expand an event record row using the dropdown arrow to inspect JSON fields. Step 26: Optimize Query Time-Range Scan Window Action / Navigation: Adjust the time-window selector (e.g., 15m, 1h) to reduce ingested bytes scanned and enhance execution speed. Step 27: Create Metric Filter from Log Group Action / Navigation: In Log groups ➔ Select /aws/ec2/system-logs ➔ Click Metric filters tab ➔ Click Create metric filter. Step 28: Define HTTP 404 Filter Pattern Action / Navigation: Configure the pattern matching syntax. Filter Pattern Syntax: [ip, user, username, timestamp, request, status_code = 404, size] 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 28:
Space-delimited patterns [field1, field2, ...] require standard Apache/Nginx combined log formatting. For JSON logs, use JSON path filters { $.status_code = 404 }. Always test patterns before saving.
Step 29: Test Filter Pattern Against Sample Logs Action / Navigation: Select sample log streams and click Test pattern. Observation: Test results verify matching lines and validate tokenized fields. Step 30: Assign Metric Name, Value, and Custom Namespace Action / Navigation: Click Next to proceed to metric naming. Configuration Parameters: Metric namespace: Custom/Web Metric name: HTTP404ErrorCount Metric value: 1 Default value: 0 Step 31: Finalize Metric Filter Provisioning Action / Navigation: Click Create metric filter. Observation: The filter is active and immediately populates the metric series HTTP404ErrorCount under All Metrics. Step 32: Configure CloudWatch Alarm on CPU Threshold (> 70%) Action / Navigation: In the sidebar, select Alarms ➔ Click Create alarm ➔ Select CPUUtilization for Web-Server-Lab. Configuration Parameters: Statistic: Average Period: 1 minute Threshold type: Static Condition: Greater > 70 Datapoints to alarm: 2 out of 2 (sustained across 2 consecutive minutes) Step 33: Configure SNS Action & Verify Alarm OK State Action / Navigation: Attach notification action pointing to an Amazon SNS Topic ➔ Name the alarm High-CPU-Utilization-Alarm ➔ Click Create alarm. Observation: The alarm initializes in healthy OK state under standard operational load. 📝 Summary & Key Takeaways: Full-Stack Observability: Amazon CloudWatch unifies the three pillars of telemetry: Metrics (telemetry timeseries), Logs (structured/unstructured events), and Alarms (automated notifications). Speed & Value of Logs Insights: Eliminates the operational overhead and infrastructure costs of self-hosted ELK stacks by querying massive log volumes serverlessly within seconds. title: Amazon SQS & DLQ Setup
content:
In this section, we set up asynchronous processing with Amazon SQS for AI question generation and validation jobs (15–45 seconds per job), consisting of a Dead-Letter Queue (exammaker-dev-ai-jobs-dlq) and a Main Queue (exammaker-dev-ai-jobs) configured with a 300-second visibility timeout, 20-second Long Polling, and a Redrive Policy (maxReceiveCount = 3).
1. Create Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) Create the Dead-Letter Queue (exammaker-dev-ai-jobs-dlq) First Open Amazon SQS in ap-southeast-1 → click Create queue. Configure the queue parameters: Type: Standard Name: exammaker-dev-ai-jobs-dlq Visibility timeout: 30 Seconds Message retention period: 14 Days (retains failed job payloads long enough for engineering root-cause analysis) Delivery delay: 0 Seconds Maximum message size: 256 KiB Receive message wait time: 0 Seconds Encryption: Enabled — Amazon SQS key (SSE-SQS) ($0). Click Create queue. 2. Create Main Queue Create the Main Queue (exammaker-dev-ai-jobs) with Long Polling & Redrive Policy In Amazon SQS, click Create queue. Configure optimal settings for the Amazon Bedrock AI Worker: Type: Standard Name: exammaker-dev-ai-jobs Visibility timeout: 300 Seconds (5 minutes) — safely exceeds the maximum Worker execution duration so SQS does not redeliver an in-progress job. Message retention period: 4 Days Delivery delay: 0 Seconds Maximum message size: 256 KiB Receive message wait time (Long Polling): 20 Seconds — eliminates ~99% of empty polling requests, staying well within the 1M free requests/month tier. Encryption: Amazon SQS key (SSE-SQS) ($0). Dead-letter queue (Redrive policy): attach exammaker-dev-ai-jobs-dlq with Maximum receives = 3. Click Create queue. 3. Set up Hybrid DNS with Route 53 Resolver: The Hybrid DNS with Route 53 Resolver (Hybrid DNS Management with Amazon Route 53) hands-on lab was conducted on Monday (12/10/2026) during Week 5. This page provides an exhaustive step-by-step implementation guide complete with precise IP CIDR allocations, nslookup validation commands, troubleshooting resolutions, and all 11 verification screenshots. 🔗 Lab Reference Material: Set up Hybrid DNS with Route 53 Resolver
🎯 Lab Objectives: Master network topology design and Hybrid DNS resolution bridging on-premises enterprise networks with AWS cloud environments. Automate multi-VPC networking infrastructure deployment via AWS CloudFormation. Configure Security Groups permitting bidirectional DNS queries (UDP and TCP Port 53) across VPC boundaries. Deploy AWS Directory Service (AWS Managed Microsoft Active Directory) acting as the authoritative on-premises enterprise DNS controller. Configure Route 53 Resolver Outbound Endpoints and Resolver Rules to conditionally forward queries originating in AWS to on-premises DNS servers. Configure Route 53 Resolver Inbound Endpoints to receive and resolve incoming queries from on-premises clients targeting AWS Private Hosted Zones. Validate end-to-end bidirectional DNS resolution using nslookup. 📊 Provisioned Resource Specifications: Resource Name / Identifier Configuration & Detailed Specs Environment / Region Notes EC2 Key Pair hybrid-dns-keypair RSA, .pem format us-east-1 Administrative access to RDGW client CloudFormation Stack Hybrid-DNS-Stack Provisions On-Prem VPC, Cloud VPC, Subnets, Route Tables, NAT GW us-east-1 Automates multi-VPC baseline environment Security Group Route53-Resolver-SG Inbound: TCP/UDP 53 (DNS), Outbound: All traffic Cloud & On-prem VPCs Secures DNS Resolver query paths Microsoft AD corp.example.com AWS Managed Microsoft AD Standard Edition On-Prem VPC Authoritative on-premises DNS controller Outbound Endpoint r53-outbound-resolver 2 IP Endpoints across 2 Availability Zones Cloud VPC Subnets Forwards AWS queries to On-Prem Resolver Forwarding Rule forward-to-corp-ad Forwards corp.example.com to Active Directory IPs Cloud VPC Association Routes on-premises domain queries Inbound Endpoint r53-inbound-resolver 2 IP Endpoints across 2 Availability Zones Cloud VPC Subnets Accepts on-premises queries to AWS Test Client EC2 RDGW-Client-Tester Windows Server 2022 / Amazon Linux Test Environment Executes nslookup validation scripts 🚀 Step-by-Step Implementation & Screenshot Gallery: Step 1: Create Administrative EC2 Key Pair (hybrid-dns-keypair) Action / Navigation: Open the Amazon EC2 console in us-east-1 (N. Virginia) ➔ In the sidebar, select Network & Security ➔ Key Pairs ➔ Click Create key pair. Configuration Parameters: Name: hybrid-dns-keypair Key pair type: RSA Private key file format: .pem (for SSH or Windows Administrator password decryption) Next Action: Click Create key pair and securely store the downloaded .pem file. Step 2: Deploy Multi-VPC Topology via AWS CloudFormation Action / Navigation: Navigate to AWS CloudFormation ➔ Click Create stack (with new resources) ➔ Select Upload a template file. Configuration Parameters: Stack name: Hybrid-DNS-Stack Parameters: Select Key Pair hybrid-dns-keypair created in Step 1 Purpose: Automatically provisions two isolated VPCs (simulated Cloud VPC 10.0.0.0/16 and On-premises VPC 192.168.0.0/16), establishes VPC Peering, Internet Gateways, Subnets, and Route Tables. Step 3: Select Security Group for Route 53 Resolver Endpoints Action / Navigation: Navigate to EC2 Console ➔ Under Network & Security ➔ Select Security Groups. Selection: Locate the designated Security Group named Route53-Resolver-SG (created by CloudFormation for Resolver endpoints). Step 4: Configure Inbound Rules (Allow Port 53 UDP & TCP) Action / Navigation: Select the Inbound rules tab ➔ Click Edit inbound rules. Configuration Parameters: Rule 1: Type DNS (UDP), Port 53, Source: On-premises VPC CIDR (192.168.0.0/16) and Cloud VPC CIDR (10.0.0.0/16) Rule 2: Type DNS (TCP), Port 53, Source: On-premises VPC CIDR (192.168.0.0/16) and Cloud VPC CIDR (10.0.0.0/16) Next Action: Click Save rules. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 4:
A frequent pitfall is opening only UDP 53 while omitting TCP 53. Standard lightweight queries use UDP, but DNS queries exceeding 512 bytes (such as DNSSEC or large responses) automatically fallback to TCP. Without TCP 53, queries will experience intermittent timeouts. Always configure both UDP and TCP rules.
Step 5: Verify Port 53 Security Group Inbound Permissions Action / Navigation: Review the finalized Inbound rules table. Observation: Both DNS (UDP) and DNS (TCP) rules on port 53 are verified active across internal VPC ranges. Step 6: Provision AWS Managed Microsoft Active Directory Action / Navigation: Navigate to AWS Directory Service ➔ Click Set up directory ➔ Select AWS Managed Microsoft AD. Configuration Parameters: Edition: Standard Edition Directory DNS name: corp.example.com Directory NetBIOS name: CORP VPC: Select On-premises VPC (192.168.0.0/16) Subnets: Select 2 Private Subnets across distinct Availability Zones Purpose: Simulates the authoritative corporate Domain Controller and internal DNS server. Step 7: Inspect Directory Status & Note Active Directory DNS IPs Action / Navigation: Allow 15-20 minutes for directory provisioning, then open directory details. Details Recorded: Status: Active DNS address 1: 192.168.1.xxx DNS address 2: 192.168.2.xxx Note: These two DNS IP addresses represent target endpoints for Route 53 Resolver forwarding rules. Step 8: Provision Route 53 Resolver Outbound Endpoint (r53-outbound-resolver) Action / Navigation: Navigate to Amazon Route 53 ➔ Under Resolver, click Outbound endpoints ➔ Click Create outbound endpoint. Configuration Parameters: Endpoint name: r53-outbound-resolver VPC: Select Cloud VPC (10.0.0.0/16) Security Group: Select Route53-Resolver-SG verified in Step 5 IP addresses: Choose at least 2 Availability Zones, assign 1 subnet per AZ, and choose Auto-allocate IP Next Action: Click Submit. Verify operational status transitions to Operational. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 8:
Route 53 Resolver strictly mandates a minimum of two IP endpoints residing in separate Availability Zones for High Availability redundancy. Selecting only one AZ halts the wizard.
Step 9: Configure Resolver Forwarding Rule for corp.example.com Action / Navigation: In the sidebar, select Resolver ➔ Rules ➔ Click Create rule. Configuration Parameters: Rule name: forward-to-corp-ad Rule type: Forward Domain name: corp.example.com VPCs that use this rule: Associate Cloud VPC Outbound endpoint: Select r53-outbound-resolver Target IP addresses: Enter the 2 Microsoft AD DNS IP addresses recorded in Step 7 (Port 53) Next Action: Click Submit. Step 10: Provision Route 53 Resolver Inbound Endpoint (r53-inbound-resolver) Action / Navigation: In the sidebar, select Resolver ➔ Inbound endpoints ➔ Click Create inbound endpoint. Configuration Parameters: Endpoint name: r53-inbound-resolver VPC: Select Cloud VPC (10.0.0.0/16) Security Group: Select Route53-Resolver-SG IP addresses: Choose 2 Availability Zones and matching subnets Purpose: Exposes static private IP addresses within AWS for on-premises DNS conditional forwarders to query AWS Private Hosted Zones (e.g., aws.local). Step 11: Validate Bidirectional DNS Resolution via nslookup Action / Navigation: Connect to the test instance (RDGW or Linux test client) and execute bidirectional DNS lookups. Commands Executed: # 1. Query on-premises domain from AWS Cloud via Outbound Endpoint nslookup dc01.corp.example.com # 2. Query AWS private hosted zone from On-premises via Inbound Endpoint nslookup app.aws.local <Inbound-Endpoint-IP> Output: Both lookups return resolved internal IP addresses without NXDOMAIN errors or timeouts, confirming seamless bidirectional Hybrid DNS operation. 📝 Summary & Key Takeaways: Seamless Hybrid DNS Architecture: Route 53 Resolver delivers an enterprise-grade DNS bridge, completely replacing burdensome, self-managed BIND forwarder instances on EC2. Clear Inbound vs Outbound Demarcation: Inbound Endpoint: Ingests external on-premises DNS queries into AWS to resolve Private Hosted Zones. Outbound Endpoint: Forwards internal AWS queries out to on-premises DNS controllers via Resolver Rules. Migration Acceleration: Enables migrating cloud workloads to interact with legacy on-premises databases, SAP, and ERP systems using standard internal domain names without rewriting network configuration strings. Hybrid Cloud Networking Architecture: Understood the DNS resolution challenge when bridging traditional on-premises enterprise data centers with AWS Cloud environments. Bidirectional DNS Routing: Mastered the core principles of Route 53 Resolver Inbound and Outbound Endpoints to enable seamless domain lookup across both networks. Validation & Troubleshooting: Verified low-latency domain lookup and end-to-end name resolution accuracy using nslookup across multi-VPC enterprise topologies. 📌 Tuesday (13/10/2026) - Command Line Operations with AWS CLI: The Command Line Operations with AWS CLI workshop was conducted on Tuesday (13/10/2026) as part of Week 5. This page provides comprehensive documentation of reviewing default service quotas, initiating an account-level quota increase request for EC2 Spot Instances (All Standard (A, C, D, H, I, M, R, T, Z) Spot Instance Requests, Quota code L-34B43A08) from 32 to 64 vCPUs in the us-east-1 region, analyzing cloud cost implications, tracking the resolution lifecycle via AWS Support Center (Case ID: 179257232100832), receiving formal confirmation emails from Amazon Web Services, and automating quota queries with the AWS CLI.
🎯 Lab Objectives: Understand the core concept and strategic role of AWS Service Quotas in enterprise cloud governance, billing safeguard enforcement, and account infrastructure defense. Distinguish between Soft Limits (service limits that can be increased via request) and Hard Limits (immutable physical or architectural boundaries enforced by AWS). Master the modern Amazon EC2 quota paradigm: understanding how AWS calculates computing thresholds based on cumulative vCPUs rather than raw server instance counts. Learn the inter-service communication workflow between customer accounts and the AWS Support Center under the Basic Support Plan. Resolve a fundamental cloud economics (Cloud FinOps) dilemma: Does requesting or getting approved for a Service Quota increase incur any financial charges? Leverage the AWS CLI (aws service-quotas) to automate quota discovery, query specific limits, inspect historical change requests, and script compliance validation. Establish Proactive Quota Monitoring by designing CloudWatch Alarms that notify operators when resource consumption approaches 80% and 95% of the allocated ceiling. 📊 Provisioned Resource Specifications: Parameter / Resource Actual Value Technical Significance & Role AWS Service Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) Core compute service providing scalable virtual computing capacity in the cloud Quota Name All Standard (A, C, D, H, I, M, R, T, Z) Spot Instance Requests Cumulative vCPU threshold for standard compute-family Spot Instances Quota Code L-34B43A08 Canonical AWS identifier for standard Spot vCPU allocation Target Region us-east-1 (US East - N. Virginia) AWS geographic region where the quota applies Default Quota Value 32 vCPUs Out-of-the-box ceiling configured by AWS for the account Requested Quota Value 64 vCPUs New requested compute ceiling submitted for AWS approval Support Case ID 179257232100832 Automated case tracking identifier created in AWS Support Center Account Support Plan Basic Support Standard non-paid support tier included with all AWS accounts Resolution Status Case Closed / Approved Request successfully validated and granted by AWS technical engineers Propagation Time Within 30 minutes Time required to synchronize the new quota across global distributed fleets Notification Channel Official email from Amazon Web Services Administrator inbox receiving official approval verification 📋 Detailed Step-by-Step Implementation Guide: 🔹 Module 1: Exploring AWS Service Quotas & Inspecting EC2 Limits Step 1: Navigate to the AWS Service Quotas Console Action: Sign in to the AWS Management Console ➔ Type Service Quotas into the top search bar ➔ Select Service Quotas from the services list. Verify Region: Confirm in the top navigation bar that the active region is US East (N. Virginia) us-east-1. Note that the vast majority of AWS infrastructure quotas are enforced independently per geographic region (Per-Region Quotas). Objective: The Service Quotas dashboard provides a centralized pane of glass to view default values, current applied values, and utilization percentages across over 250 AWS services. Step 2: Navigate to Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) Action: On the left navigation pane, click AWS services ➔ In the service filter search box, enter EC2 or Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) ➔ Click the service name to inspect its catalog of configurable quotas. Observation: EC2 manages hundreds of distinct quotas covering Elastic IPs, VPC Peering limits, Launch Templates, and vCPU quotas categorized by instance families (Standard, High Memory, Accelerated Computing) and pricing models (On-Demand vs Spot). Step 3: Filter for the Standard Spot vCPU Quota Action: In the quota search box (Filter quotas), enter: All Standard (A, C, D, H, I, M, R, T, Z) Spot Instance Requests. Displayed Metadata: Quota name: All Standard (A, C, D, H, I, M, R, T, Z) Spot Instance Requests Quota code: L-34B43A08 Default value: 32 (vCPUs) Applied value: 32 (vCPUs) Significance: This quota dictates that within us-east-1, the account can run concurrent standard Spot instances up to a collective sum of 32 vCPUs. For example, 16 instances of t3.medium (2 vCPUs x 16 = 32 vCPUs) or 4 instances of c5.2xlarge (8 vCPUs x 4 = 32 vCPUs). 🔹 Module 2: Submitting a Quota Increase Request Step 4: Open Request Modal and Test Input Validation Action: Select the All Standard (A, C, D, H, I, M, R, T, Z) Spot Instance Requests entry ➔ Click the orange Request increase at account level button. Modal Context: The dialog displays: Description: The maximum number of vCPUs for all running or requested Standard (A, C, D, H, I, M, R, T, Z) Spot Instances per Region. Requested for: Account ID 887086382708. Region: United States (N. Virginia) us-east-1. Testing Input Validation: In the Increase quota value field, enter 32 (matching the current limit). Console Feedback: An immediate red client-side validation error is triggered: ❌ Must be a number greater than your current quota value of 32
Technical Takeaway: AWS enforces robust UI-level validation to prevent redundant, no-op support ticket submissions. Step 5: Input Target Limit of 64 vCPUs and Submit Input Parameter: Increase quota value: Enter 64 (doubling compute capacity to support parallel distributed workloads with Spot cost savings). AWS Approval Notice: ℹ️ Approvals: For some services, smaller increases are automatically approved, while larger requests are partially approved or routed to AWS Support for engineering review.
Action: Click Request to transmit the formal quota increase application. 🔹 Module 3: Tracking Approval Lifecycle and Verifying Resolution Step 6: Monitor Progress via the Service Quotas Dashboard Action: Return to the primary Service Quotas console ➔ Navigate to Dashboard or Quota request history. Propagation Window: A propagation window of approximately 30 minutes is allocated for worldwide distributed control planes to complete consistency synchronization. 🔹 Module 4: Managing Service Quotas Programmatically via AWS CLI In addition to Console workflows, cloud infrastructure engineers automate service quota audits and limit requests using the AWS CLI v2.
Step 9: Query Service Codes for EC2 Discover canonical service identifiers:
aws service-quotas list-services \ --query "Services[?contains(ServiceCode, 'ec2')].{Code:ServiceCode, Name:ServiceName}" \ --output table Step 10: Query Current Spot vCPU Limit via Quota Code L-34B43A08 Inspect the active value in us-east-1:
aws service-quotas get-service-quota \ --service-code ec2 \ --quota-code L-34B43A08 \ --region us-east-1 \ --query "Quota.{QuotaName:QuotaName, QuotaCode:QuotaCode, Value:Value, Unit:Unit, Adjustable:Adjustable}" \ --output json Sample JSON Response: { "QuotaName": "All Standard (A, C, D, H, I, M, R, T, Z) Spot Instance Requests", "QuotaCode": "L-34B43A08", "Value": 64.0, "Unit": "None", "Adjustable": true } Analysis: The "Value": 64.0 field confirms system-wide convergence on the 64 vCPU limit, while "Adjustable": true confirms this is an elastic soft quota. Step 11: Scripting Automated Quota Increase Requests Submit a quota adjustment programmatically:
aws service-quotas request-service-quota-increase \ --service-code ec2 \ --quota-code L-34B43A08 \ --desired-value 64 \ --region us-east-1 Step 12: Inspecting Quota Request History via CLI Audit the status of historical submissions:
aws service-quotas list-requested-service-quota-change-history-by-quota \ --service-code ec2 \ --quota-code L-34B43A08 \ --region us-east-1 \ --query "RequestedQuotas[*].{ID:Id, Status:Status, DesiredValue:DesiredValue, Created:Created}" \ --output table 🔹 Module 5: Proactive Limit Monitoring with CloudWatch Alarms To safeguard auto-scaling groups and distributed jobs against unexpected throttling exceptions, production architectures pair Service Quotas with CloudWatch Alarms:
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \ --alarm-name "EC2-Spot-vCPU-Quota-Utilization-High" \ --alarm-description "Trigger alarm when Spot vCPU utilization exceeds 80% of the 64 vCPU ceiling" \ --namespace "AWS/Usage" \ --metric-name "ResourceCount" \ --dimensions Name=Service,Value=EC2 Name=Type,Value=Resource Name=Resource,Value=SpotInstances \ --statistic Maximum \ --period 300 \ --threshold 51.2 \ --comparison-operator GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold \ --evaluation-periods 1 \ --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:887086382708:aws-cli 💡 Troubleshooting & Real-World Lessons: 1. Cloud Economics Question: Does increasing a Service Quota from 32 to 64 vCPUs incur billing charges? Technical Reality: ABSOLUTELY NOT. AWS Billing Model: A Service Quota is purely a “safety ceiling” designed to prevent runaway costs caused by operational mistakes, runaway scripts, or security breaches. Submitting an increase request and having it approved to 64 vCPUs is 100% free of charge. AWS only bills for actual compute consumption—measuring seconds of active instance runtime. If your account holds a limit of 64 vCPUs but runs 0 active instances, your EC2 bill remains exactly $0.00. 2. Client-Side Input Validation (“Must be a number greater than your current quota value of 32”) Root Cause: Attempting to submit a request with the value 32, identical to the active baseline. Resolution: Submissions must specify a positive integer strictly higher than the current value (e.g., 64 or 128). Values must be backed by architectural requirements to avoid administrative review rejections. 3. Differentiating Soft Quotas vs. Hard Quotas Soft Quotas: Administrative safeguards that can be adjusted via Service Quotas or AWS Support tickets (e.g., EC2 vCPUs, Elastic IP allocations, DynamoDB provisioned capacity). Hard Quotas: Immutable architectural or protocol limits fixed by AWS service design (e.g., DynamoDB maximum item size of 400 KB, SQS payload maximum of 256 KB, maximum VPC peering connections per route table). 4. Regional Scope of Quotas (Per-Region Quotas) Observation: Increasing the Spot vCPU quota to 64 in us-east-1 (N. Virginia) leaves other regions (e.g., ap-southeast-1 Singapore) at their default 32 vCPU limit. Best Practice: In multi-region deployments or disaster recovery configurations, quota adjustments must be initiated and tracked independently for each designated target region. 5. Shift from Instance-Count Limits to vCPU-Based Quotas Historical Context: Historically, AWS throttled EC2 instances by gross instance count (e.g., 20 instances). This treated a lightweight t3.nano (2 vCPUs, 0.5 GB RAM) identically to a massive c5.18xlarge (72 vCPUs, 144 GB RAM). Modern Model: By measuring raw vCPU capacity, organizations enjoy granular elasticity to deploy diverse instance combinations up to their aggregate compute ceiling. 6. Propagation Delay (~30 Minutes) Behavior: Attempting to launch instances immediately following ticket closure might briefly yield MaxSpotInstanceCountExceeded errors. Mechanism: AWS operates a massive global control plane. A brief 15 to 30-minute consistency window is necessary for the new capacity quota to replicate to every placement engine across Availability Zones. 7. Account Justification for High-Volume Increases Risk Management: For new AWS accounts, AWS enforces conservative baseline limits to mitigate fraudulent activity, unauthorized cryptocurrency mining, or DDoS botnet creation. Operational Tip: When requesting high-magnitude quota jumps, provide clear use-case justifications in the description field (e.g., “Training deep learning models for university capstone research”). 8. Automated Multi-Account Quota Templates Enterprise Scaling: Organizations utilizing AWS Organizations can configure Quota Request Templates. When new member accounts are provisioned, approved quota increases are automatically requested across all member environments without manual administrative intervention. 📌 Summary & Skills Acquired: Through the Resource Limit Governance with AWS Service Quotas lab, the intern has acquired:
Thorough comprehension of resource quota governance on the AWS cloud platform. Complete practical execution of the vCPU quota increase lifecycle (L-34B43A08) from 32 to 64 vCPUs. Cohesive integration between the Service Quotas Console, AWS Support Center, and Email notification channels. Technical Support Case Integration (AWS Support Center): Experienced case management lifecycle, support notifications, and official email confirmations under the Basic Support tier. CLI Automation & Proactive Monitoring: Practiced command-line quota auditing and planned CloudWatch alarm thresholds to prevent compute exhaustion before reaching capacity limits. 📌 Results for Tuesday (20/10/2026) - Optimize Amazon EC2 Costs with AWS Lambda & Slack Notifications: The Optimize Amazon EC2 Costs with AWS Lambda & Slack Notifications hands-on lab was conducted on Tuesday (20/10/2026) as part of Week 6. Step 11: Access Grafana Web UI & Update Admin Password Action: Open a web browser and navigate to http://44.203.10.190:3000. Initial Authentication: Authenticate with initial credentials admin / admin. Part 4: CloudWatch Data Source & Dashboard Visualization Step 12: Add CloudWatch Data Source & Validate API Connectivity Action: In Grafana’s left navigation bar, choose Connections ➔ Data sources ➔ Click Add new data source ➔ Select CloudWatch. Configuration: Authentication Provider: Select AWS SDK Default (leveraging the attached EC2 instance role without static credentials). Default Region: Set to us-east-1 (or target workload region). Connection Test: Click Save & test. The green notification confirms: 1. Successfully queried the CloudWatch metrics API. 2. Successfully queried the CloudWatch logs API. Step 13: Build Time-Series Monitoring Dashboard for CPU Utilization Action: Navigate to Dashboards ➔ Click New dashboard ➔ Select Add visualization ➔ Choose cloudwatch. Query Builder Parameters: Namespace: AWS/EC2. Metric name: CPUUtilization. Statistic: Average. Dimensions: Filter by InstanceId = i-082d165f34a40407f. Step 14: Advanced Metric Exploration with Explore Tool Action: In the main menu, click Explore ➔ Select cloudwatch data source. Ad-hoc Query: Target region: ap-southeast-1. Metric: CPUUtilization, Dimension: InstanceId = i-0ba9a1a9ccab2d73f. Switch visualization mode to Bars to highlight workload spikes with distinct clarity. 💡 Lessons Learned & Troubleshooting Bank: Below are 5 practical troubleshooting scenarios encountered during Grafana and CloudWatch deployment, accompanied by verified root causes and solutions:
1. Inability to Access Grafana Web UI on Port 3000 (Connection Timed Out) Root Cause: The EC2 Security Group lacked an Inbound rule permitting TCP traffic on port 3000 from client IP ranges, or the instance was provisioned in an isolated subnet lacking an Internet Gateway route. Remediation: Inspect SG-PUB-Grafana-ASG Inbound rules and verify that Custom TCP on port 3000 is open. Confirm the subnet route table points 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway (igw-xxxx). 2. CloudWatch Data Source Authorization Error (AccessDeniedException / HTTP 403) Root Cause: The IAM Role attached to the EC2 instance lacked permissions required to invoke CloudWatch or CloudWatch Logs metric queries. Remediation: Ensure GrafanaAccessPolicy includes complete read-only actions: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowGrafanaCloudWatchAccess", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "cloudwatch:DescribeAlarmsForMetric", "cloudwatch:DescribeAlarmHistory", "cloudwatch:DescribeAlarms", "cloudwatch:ListMetrics", "cloudwatch:GetMetricStatistics", "cloudwatch:GetMetricData", "logs:DescribeLogGroups", "logs:GetLogGroupFields", "logs:StartQuery", "logs:StopQuery", "logs:GetQueryResults", "logs:GetLogEvents", "ec2:DescribeTags", "ec2:DescribeInstances", "ec2:DescribeRegions" ], "Resource": "*" } ] } 3. Best Practice: EC2 IAM Instance Profile vs Static Access Keys Analysis: Hard-coding IAM user Access Key ID and Secret Access Key into web application configuration violates the principle of least privilege and introduces credential exposure risks. Architectural Guidance: Always use AWS SDK Default authentication on AWS-hosted Grafana instances. Grafana retrieves rotating, temporary tokens via the Instance Metadata Service (IMDSv2) automatically. 4. grafana-server Service Fails to Start Automatically on Instance Reboot Root Cause: Administrator manually executed systemctl start grafana-server without enabling the systemd service unit. Remediation: Always run sudo systemctl enable grafana-server. Confirm configuration via systemctl is-enabled grafana-server (expected output: enabled). 5. Clean-Up Lifecycle to Prevent Cloud Charges (Resource Cleanup) Decommissioning Steps: Terminate the EC2 host Grafana-Server (i-082d165f34a40407f). Detach and delete GrafanaAccessRole and GrafanaAccessPolicy. Delete security group SG-PUB-Grafana-ASG. Delete the custom VPC Grafana-ASG-vpc to release associated subnets and Internet Gateway resources. Grafana Server Deployment on AL2023: Provisioned open-source Grafana v13.3.0 on Amazon Linux 2023, configuring official RPM repositories and managing services with systemd. Credential-less CloudWatch Integration: Utilized EC2 Instance Profile (GrafanaAccessRole) adhering to AWS Zero-Trust guidelines without embedding static API keys. title: CloudWatch & SNS Monitoring Setup
content:
In this section, we build a proactive monitoring and alerting stack at $0/month (100% within AWS Free Tier): an SNS Topic (exammaker-dev-alerts), a 7-day CloudWatch Log Group (/exammaker/dev/app) with 4 Metric Filters, and exactly 10/10 Standard CloudWatch Alarms.
1. Create SNS Topic & Email Subscription Step 1: Create the exammaker-dev-alerts SNS Topic Open Amazon SNS in ap-southeast-1 → select Topics → Create topic. Configure: Type: Standard Name: exammaker-dev-alerts Display name: ExamMakerAlert (Max message size: 256 KiB) Click Create topic. Step 2: Subscribe Operations Team Emails Inside the exammaker-dev-alerts topic, click Create subscription. Select Protocol: Email and enter the engineering team email addresses (4 email subscribers). Click Confirm subscription in each confirmation email so the status transitions to Confirmed. 2. Create 7-Day Log Group & Metric Filters Step 1: Create /exammaker/dev/app Log Group with 7-Day Retention Open Amazon CloudWatch → Logs → Log groups → Create log group. Configure: Log group name: /exammaker/dev/app Retention setting: 1 week (7 days) (keeps log storage well under the 5 GB free tier cap) Log class: Standard Step 2: Create 4 Metric Filters Under Namespace ExamMaker/Dev Inside /exammaker/dev/app, open Metric filters → Create metric filter to publish 4 operational metrics into namespace ExamMaker/Dev (Metric value = 1, Unit = Count):
Api5xxCount (tracks HTTP 5xx server errors from the backend API) WorkerHeartbeat (verifies the background AI Worker process is alive) StuckRunningJobs (detects jobs stuck in Running state) WorkerErrorCount (counts unhandled Worker exceptions during Bedrock / RDS calls) 3. Configure & Verify 10 CloudWatch Alarms Complete Set of 10/10 Standard CloudWatch Alarms (Period = 300s — Free Tier $0) All 10 alarms route notifications to the exammaker-dev-alerts SNS Topic and report 100% OK status:
exammaker-dev-worker-heartbeat: < 1 over 5 minutes exammaker-dev-worker-errors: >= 3 errors over 5 minutes exammaker-dev-api-5xx: >= 5 HTTP 5xx responses over 5 minutes exammaker-dev-ebs-stalled-io: > 0 stalled I/O events on the root EBS volume exammaker-dev-worker-stuck-jobs: > 0 stuck jobs over 5 minutes exammaker-dev-rds-connections-high: > 50 database connections exammaker-dev-sqs-dlq-depth: > 0 messages in the Dead-Letter Queue exammaker-dev-sqs-oldest-msg: oldest message age > 600s (10 minutes) exammaker-dev-ec2-cpu-high: CPU utilization > 80% for 10 minutes (2 x 5m) exammaker-dev-rds-storage-low: free storage space < 2 GB (2,147,483,648 bytes)

title: Clean up
content:
This guide covers the complete teardown procedure for all AI Exam Maker infrastructure resources in the ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) region after completing the demo and project evaluation, ensuring zero unexpected background charges.
Operational Note (if only pausing overnight before the demo day): When you only choose Stop temporarily on Amazon RDS (exammaker-dev-pg), AWS keeps the stopped state for a maximum of 7 days and will automatically restart the database after 7 days, resuming hourly billing. Therefore, once the workshop / demo is finished, you must execute the complete Cleanup procedure in the dependency order below.
Step 1: Empty and Delete Storage S3 Buckets Amazon S3 does not allow deleting a non-empty bucket directly, so each bucket must be emptied (Empty) before deletion (Delete):
Open Amazon S3 → in the left navigation pane, select General purpose buckets (1). Select the 2 project buckets in the ap-southeast-1 region one by one (2): exam-maker-frontend-cloudmiracle (static frontend) and aem-dev-backend-artifacts-9d07a0f131 (backend release artifacts). Click Empty (3) → enter permanently delete to remove all objects and versions inside. Return to the bucket list, select the bucket again, and click Delete (4) to permanently remove the bucket. Step 2: Delete Amazon RDS PostgreSQL Database & Check Snapshots Open Aurora and RDS → in the left navigation pane, select Databases (1). Select the exammaker-dev-pg (PostgreSQL, db.t4g.micro) instance (2) (Note: if Deletion protection was enabled before the demo, click Modify → uncheck Enable deletion protection → select Apply immediately before deleting). Click Actions (3) → select Delete (4). In the Delete exammaker-dev-pg instance confirmation dialog: Uncheck Create final snapshot (avoids $0.095/GB-month snapshot storage fees). Uncheck Retain automated backups (prevents retaining billable automated backups after deletion). Type delete me into the confirmation field and click Delete. Additional Check (Manual Snapshots): Manual snapshots created before major migrations or recovery drills are not automatically deleted when the DB instance is removed. After the step above, go to Snapshots → Manual tab in the left menu and delete any remaining project snapshots via Actions → Delete snapshot.
Step 3: Terminate EC2 Instance & Check Unattached EBS Volumes Open EC2 → in the left navigation pane, select Instances (1). Check the aem-exammaker-ec2 (t4g.small) instance (2). Click Instance state (next to Actions) (3) → select Terminate (delete) instance (4). In the Terminate (delete) instance confirmation dialog, verify Termination protection: Disabled and the default notice stating that the root EBS volume (30 GiB gp3) will be automatically deleted with the instance, then click Terminate (delete). Additional Check (Unattached EBS Volumes): Once the EC2 instance transitions completely to Terminated, open Elastic Block Store → Volumes in the left menu and filter by Volume state = Available (detached volumes not attached to any instance). If any Available volumes remain, select Actions → Delete volume to avoid $0.096/GB-month storage charges.
Step 4: Release Static Elastic IP Address — Most Important AWS charges $0.005/hour (~$3.65/month) for every Public IPv4 / Elastic IP address allocated to an account, even after the associated EC2 instance has been terminated.
In the EC2 console, scroll down the left menu to Network & Security → Elastic IPs (1). Check the project’s aem-exammaker-eip (13.251.22.203) address (2) (ensure this is performed after the EC2 instance reaches Terminated, or select Actions → Disassociate Elastic IP address first). Click Actions (3) → select Release Elastic IP addresses (4) → click Release to return the IP address to AWS. Step 5: Audit High-Cost Network Resources & Clean Up Supporting Services Verify Zero Load Balancers & NAT Gateways: Check EC2 → Load Balancing → Load Balancers to confirm the list is empty (0 load balancers). Check VPC → NAT gateways to confirm the list is empty (0 NAT gateways — adhering to the $200 budget-optimized architecture). Clean Up Remaining Configuration & Monitoring Services (Account Hygiene): Amazon Route 53 (if using an AWS Hosted Zone): open Hosted zones, delete the project’s custom A/CNAME records, and delete the Hosted Zone (avoiding the fixed $0.50/month/zone maintenance fee). Amazon CloudWatch & SNS: delete the /exammaker/dev/app Log Group, delete the 10 exammaker-dev-* Alarms, and delete the exammaker-dev-alerts SNS Topic. Amazon SQS: delete the 2 queues exammaker-dev-ai-jobs and exammaker-dev-ai-jobs-dlq. Amazon Cognito: delete the exammaker-dev-users User Pool. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: delete configuration parameters under /exammaker/dev/* and /exammaker-ops/dev/*. IAM & VPC: delete the project IAM roles (aem-exammaker-ec2-role, aem-github-*-deploy-role) and delete the aem-demo-vpc VPC (associated free Subnets, Route Tables, Internet Gateway, and Security Groups will be removed along with the VPC). Final Verification: after 24 hours, open AWS Billing and Cost Management → Bills to confirm no services continue accruing hourly charges.

Deploy Standard vs FIFO SQS queues and reduce polling costs using Long Polling (20s). - Configure Visibility Timeout and Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ) with Redrive Policies. 16/11/2026 16/11/2026 Serverless Workshop (000078) Tuesday Pub/Sub Routing (SNS/EventBridge) & AWS Step Functions: - Build a Fanout architecture fanning one SNS Topic to multiple independent SQS Queues. - Configure Amazon EventBridge Event Buses with JSON Event Pattern Filtering rules. - Design State Machines in Workflow Studio combining Task, Choice, Parallel, and Retry/Catch logic. 17/11/2026 17/11/2026 Cloud Journey - Modernize Wednesday Docker Multi-Stage, Amazon ECR & Amazon ECS Fargate: - Author optimized Multi-Stage Dockerfiles running under a non-root user. - Push images to private Amazon ECR with Lifecycle Policies and CVE Scan on Push. - Enable IAM OIDC Provider for pod-level least-privilege permissions (IRSA). - Install AWS Load Balancer Controller (ALB Ingress), Metrics Server, and configure HPA pod scaling. 19/11/2026 19/11/2026 Amazon EKS Workshop (000126) Friday Week 10 Review, Worklog & Project: - Hardening Amazon API Gateway & Decoupling with Amazon SQS What did I learn today? Amazon API Gateway (REST vs HTTP API): HTTP API delivers lower latency and >70% cost savings for lightweight microservices, while REST API provides Usage Plans, API Keys, WAF integration, and Private Endpoints. Implemented a Lambda Custom Authorizer for JWT validation and configured Rate/Burst Throttling. Asynchronous Decoupling with Amazon SQS: Contrasted Standard Queues (at-least-once, near-unlimited throughput) with FIFO Queues (exactly-once, ordered per MessageGroupId). Configured Long Polling (ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds = 20), VisibilityTimeout = 30s, and a DLQ Redrive Policy (maxReceiveCount = 3). Challenges & Resolutions: Browser CORS rejections & duplicate worker processing: Enabled OPTIONS preflight methods with explicit Access-Control-Allow-* headers on API Gateway, and called change_message_visibility dynamically for long-running jobs exceeding 30s. 📌 Tuesday (17/11/2026) - Amazon SNS Fanout, EventBridge & AWS Step Functions What did I learn today? SNS Fanout & EventBridge Content Filtering: Subscribed multiple SQS queues to a single SNS Topic for parallel downstream processing, and configured JSON content-based EventBridge routing rules: { "source": ["app.events"], "detail-type": ["JobSubmitted"], "detail": { "priority": ["HIGH"] } } Workflow Orchestration with AWS Step Functions: Built Amazon States Language (ASL) workflows combining Task, Choice, and Parallel states with exponential backoff Retry (BackoffRate = 2.0) and Catch compensating branches. Challenges & Resolutions: Empty SQS queues after SNS publish & state payload mismatches: Granted sqs:SendMessage to the SNS Topic ARN in the SQS Access Policy, and applied InputPath, ResultPath, and OutputPath JSONPath filters between Step Functions states. 📌 Wednesday (18/11/2026) - Docker Multi-Stage, Amazon ECR & Amazon ECS Fargate What did I learn today? Lean Container Builds & Amazon ECR: Separated compile-time dependencies (builder stage) from minimal runtime images (alpine/distroless) with USER appuser (non-root), shrinking image size and attack surface while enabling ECR Lifecycle Policies and Scan on Push. aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 887086382708.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com docker build -t fcaj/backend-api:v1.0 . docker tag fcaj/backend-api:v1.0 887086382708.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/fcaj/backend-api:v1.0 docker push 887086382708.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/fcaj/backend-api:v1.0 Serverless Containers on Amazon ECS Fargate: Strictly separated the Task Execution Role (ECR pulls & CloudWatch log delivery) from the Task Role (application AWS permissions), deploying behind an ALB with Minimum healthy percent = 100% and Maximum percent = 200% for zero-downtime rolling updates.
